title: The Practice: Your Fascia Exercise Library
tagline: Eight simple, at-home practices that train your body as one connected, springy system, starting from the feet.
intro_markdown:
## Theory is over. Now you train.

You've learned what fascia is, how the lines connect your foot to your glute and your hip to the opposite shoulder, and why so much modern gym training ignores it. This module is where you put it into practice.

Every lesson here is one exercise or one short routine. You can do almost all of them at home, barefoot, with no equipment. A wall, a doorframe or a pull-up bar, and maybe a foam roller, is all you'll need.

## How this library is built

The lessons follow the body from the ground up:

1. **Foot & Toe Wake-Up**, the foundation
2. **Feet Straight: Stance & Walk**, alignment you carry all day
3. **Pogo Hops & Wall Bounces**, your elastic spring
4. **The Flying Sword**, loading the back line like a bow
5. **The Big Cat Stretch & Octopus Leg**, slow stretches through long lines
6. **Spiral Reach & Rotation**, waking the spiral line
7. **Crawl & Hang**, ground and overhead
8. **Slow Rolling**, self-myofascial release done the fascia way

Each lesson gives you: **How to do it, Sets & timing, Progressions, Why it works, Common mistakes,** and a **Safety note.**

## Where the methods come from

- **Coach Chong Xie** is our primary voice for foot-driven, fascia-first athleticism. *Secret of Athleticism* is his brand and website, and his YouTube channel is "Coach Chong Xie" (@HyperarchFasciaTraining). He created Hyperarch Fascia Training (HFT). Parts of HFT are paid (a kit, a premium plan, Patreon and coaching), so we don't reproduce his program here. We link his free videos so you can learn his versions straight from him.
- **GOATA** is a movement system founded by Coach Gil (Jose Guillermo Boesch). Its "Global Laws" include *Feet Straight*, *Inside Ankle Bone High* and *Back Chain Dominant*. **Nick Ball Training** is a YouTube channel that teaches GOATA-style squats, feet and walking drills.
- **Robert Schleip and Divo Müller's Fascial Fitness** principles give us the scientific backbone: elastic recoil, preparatory counter-movement, slow and fast dynamic stretching, proprioceptive refinement, and hydration.

## The golden rules

- **Little and often beats big and rare.** Müller and Schleip suggest that a few minutes of fascia-oriented exercise once or twice a week is enough to drive collagen remodelling, and that the renewal takes between six months and two years. Foot work can be daily.
- **Quiet is the cue.** If a hop or a landing is loud, you're using brute muscle and collapsing. Springy and silent means your fascia is doing the work.
- **Feel, don't force.** No jerking and no pain. Movement should feel fluid, even pleasurable.
- **This adds to your training, it doesn't replace it.** Müller and Schleip say themselves that fascial training should not replace strength, cardiovascular and coordination work. It's an addition to a complete program.

## A sample week

- **Daily (5–10 min):** Foot & Toe Wake-Up, plus a few minutes of Feet Straight standing and walking.
- **2× per week (15–20 min):** Pogo Hops → Flying Sword → Big Cat Stretch → Spiral Reach → Crawl & Hang.
- **As needed (5–10 min):** Slow Rolling on tight or stiff areas, ideally on easy days.

This is Josh's philosophy: your body is one piece, and you train it like one. These are the simple practices he used to leave the physio's table behind. Start small, stay consistent, and let the tissue change.

> **Safety first:** This course is education, not medical advice. If you have a current injury, pain that doesn't settle, a heart or circulatory condition, osteoporosis, are pregnant, or are recovering from surgery, check with a qualified clinician before starting.

lessons.title: Foot & Toe Wake-Up: Rebuild Your Foundation
lessons.summary: Every fascial line starts at the ground. A short daily barefoot routine of toe spreading, short-foot holds and toe curls wakes up the small muscles and the springy tissue that most shoes have switched off.
lessons.body_markdown:
## Why we start at the feet

Your feet are your first contact with the ground on every step, jump and cut. Coach Chong Xie built his whole system around this idea. He describes Hyperarch Fascia Training as coming from his original work on the "hyperarch mechanism" in the fascially molded feet of elite athletes, and he calls fascia "the power source, the missing link." You'll hear him talk about the **foot-to-glute connection**: a strong, tensioned foot links up the chain to the hips.

You don't have to buy into every detail of his system to see the core idea. Weak, "switched-off" feet put more load on everything above them.

## How to do it

Do this barefoot, on a firm floor. Sit for the first round, then progress to standing.

**1. Toe spread (30 seconds)**
Spread your toes as wide as you can, as if you're making space between every toe. Hold 3–5 seconds, relax, repeat. If you can't spread them at all, don't worry. That's the point of the drill.

**2. Short foot (5–8 reps, hold 5–10 seconds)**
Keep your toes long and relaxed. Gently draw the ball of your foot toward your heel without curling the toes, so the arch lifts a little. Imagine "shortening" the foot. This is the classic *short foot exercise* that clinicians use to train the small (intrinsic) foot muscles.

**3. Big toe press / little toes lift (8–10 reps)**
Press your big toe into the floor while lifting the other four. Then swap: lift the big toe, press the little toes down. It's tricky at first. Go slow.

**4. Toe curls (8–12 reps)**
Curl your toes firmly into the floor (or scrunch a towel toward you), hold 2–3 seconds, release. Chong Xie has a whole video on an *elevated toe curl* variation. Watch it to see his version and cues.

**5. Barefoot time**
Spend some of your day barefoot at home. Walk around, stand while you cook, feel the floor.

## Sets & timing

- **5–10 minutes, daily** (or at least 5 days a week).
- 1–2 rounds of the sequence above.
- For reference: in a 2024 randomized trial (Gabriel and colleagues), participants did 2 × 6 minutes of foot exercises twice a day, at least five days a week, for four weeks, and improved their foot posture scores.

## Progressions

1. **Seated → standing on two feet → standing on one foot.**
2. **Single-leg balance with short foot:** hold the short foot while balancing for 20–30 seconds.
3. **Heel raises with toe control:** rise onto the balls of your feet keeping the big toe pressed down and the ankle from rolling out.
4. **Walk in minimalist or barefoot-style shoes** for part of your day, building up gradually.

## Why it works

There's solid research here:

- **Feet get stronger with simple stimulus.** In a randomized trial of 57 runners (Ridge et al., 2019), both an 8-week progressive foot-strengthening program and gradually walking more in minimalist shoes increased foot muscle size and strength. The control group didn't change. The authors also note that supportive footwear may contribute to intrinsic foot muscle weakness.
- **Toe strength links to jumping.** In 31 young men, Yamauchi and Koyama (2020) found that toe-flexor strength and its rate of force development correlated with squat jump and countermovement jump height and rebound jump performance. Arch height didn't.
- **The "foot core."** McKeon and Fourchet (2015) describe the intrinsic foot muscles as playing a critical role in absorption and propulsion. They propose a progression that starts by isolating them with the short foot exercise.

An honest caveat: the 2024 Gabriel trial found *local* changes (foot posture improved clearly, and ankle motion and balance improved in the trained leg by the follow-up), but no measurable "remote" effect up the posterior chain after four weeks. The foot-to-glute connection is central to Josh's and Chong's philosophy. The research on how much foot training alone changes the hips is still emerging. Feet first, then build up the chain, which is what the rest of this module does.

## Common mistakes

- **Curling the toes during short foot.** The toes stay long. The arch lifts because the foot shortens.
- **Rolling onto the outside edge** of the foot to fake an arch.
- **Going barefoot all day, all at once.** Feet adapt over weeks, not days.
- **Gripping with your whole body.** Keep your shoulders, jaw and breath relaxed.

## Safety note

Cramping in the arch is common at first. Stop, massage it, and come back with less effort. If you have diabetes, reduced sensation in your feet, an open wound, or a current foot injury (for example plantar heel pain or a stress fracture), get clinical advice before going barefoot or loading the feet.
key_takeaways: Do 5–10 minutes of barefoot foot work most days: toe spread, short foot, big-toe/little-toe control, toe curls.
Research shows foot muscles get bigger and stronger with simple exercise or gradual minimalist-shoe walking (Ridge et al., 2019).
Toe-flexor strength correlates with jump performance (Yamauchi & Koyama, 2020).
Research on whether foot training alone changes the hips is still emerging. Build up the chain from here.

lessons.title: Feet Straight: Stance & Walk
lessons.summary: Alignment isn't something you do for ten minutes. It's how you stand and walk all day. Learn the GOATA-inspired 'feet straight, inside ankle high' stance and carry it into your walk.
lessons.body_markdown:
## The posture you practise all day

You'll spend a few minutes a day on exercises. You spend *hours* standing and walking. If those hours are spent with collapsed arches and turned-out feet, that's the pattern your tissue adapts to.

That's the logic behind **GOATA**, a movement system founded by Coach Gil (Jose Guillermo Boesch). Sources give the acronym as *Greatest Of All Time Athletes* or *Greatest Of All Time Actions*. GOATA teaches a set of "Global Laws," including:

- **Feet Straight**: feet lined up with the body's columns
- **Inside Ankle Bone High**: don't let the ankle collapse inward
- **Back Chain Dominant**: let the posterior chain do the work
- **Head Control**: manage head and eyes for balance

GOATA's coaches teach that there's a proper alignment the body is built for. Treat that as the system's philosophy, not settled science. We found no peer-reviewed trials testing GOATA itself. But the cues are simple, free, and pair perfectly with the foot work from Lesson 1.

## How to do it

### Part A: The stance (2–3 minutes)

1. **Stand barefoot, feet about hip-width apart.**
2. **Point your feet straight ahead.** Use the outer edge of each foot or a line on the floor as a guide. For many people, "straight" will feel pigeon-toed at first.
3. **Lift the inside ankle bone.** Without curling the toes, gently raise the inner ankle so the arch isn't collapsing. Use your *short foot* from Lesson 1.
4. **Weight spread over the whole foot,** with the big toe connected to the floor.
5. **Soft knees, tall spine, eyes level.** Feel your weight slightly toward the back of the body, through the heels and hamstrings, not hanging forward on the front of the thighs.
6. **Breathe.** Hold for 30–60 seconds, rest, repeat.

### Part B: The walk (2–5 minutes)

1. Start in the stance.
2. Walk slowly with feet tracking straight ahead.
3. Keep the inside ankle high on each step.
4. Push the ground *behind* you with the back leg rather than reaching and slamming the heel out in front.
5. Stay quiet. A soft, quiet walk is a springy walk.

Watch the GOATA Movement and Nick Ball videos below. Copy what you see before reading more.

## Sets & timing

- **Daily:** 2–3 × 30–60 second stance holds + 2–5 minutes of focused walking.
- **All day:** "micro-checks." Every time you're waiting in a queue, brushing your teeth or on the phone, check: feet straight? inside ankle high?

## Progressions

1. **Stance → slow walk → normal-pace walk.**
2. **Single-leg stance** with feet straight and inside ankle high, 20–30 seconds each side.
3. **Feet-straight squat:** sit down and stand up with feet straight and arches holding. See Nick Ball's *Goata Squats for feet, ankles, & hips* below.
4. **Barefoot walks outside** on safe ground (grass, sand) once your feet are ready.

## Why it works

- **Fascia adapts to how you load it, every day.** Müller and Schleip point out that connective tissue remodels to its dominant loading patterns. Their example: through everyday walking on two legs, the fascia on the outer side of the thigh develops a palpable firmness. Your habitual stance *is* a training stimulus.
- **The feet are where the long lines begin.** Myers' Superficial Back Line runs from the underside of the toes, under the heel, up the back of the legs and spine, and over the head to the brow. A dissection-based systematic review (Wilke et al., 2016) found strong evidence that this line exists as a continuous anatomical connection. What happens at the bottom of the chain is anatomically connected to what's above it.
- **Stronger feet support the arch you're asking for.** Lesson 1's foot strength gives you the capacity to hold "inside ankle high" without straining.

## Common mistakes

- **Forcing the feet straight from the toes** while knees and hips twist. Turn the whole leg gently.
- **Locking the knees** or leaning back stiffly. Stay soft.
- **Curling the toes** to lift the arch.
- **Overdoing it on day one.** If your hips or knees ache, take a break, and build up gradually.

## Safety note

Some people have natural structural differences (for example in hip or shin rotation) that mean perfectly straight feet aren't comfortable or appropriate. Never force a position that causes pain. If you have known hip, knee or foot conditions, work with a clinician on what alignment suits you.
key_takeaways: Your all-day stance and walk are training. Fascia adapts to its dominant loading patterns.
GOATA cues: feet straight, inside ankle bone high, back-chain dominant, head control.
GOATA was founded by Coach Gil (Jose Guillermo Boesch); its claims haven't been tested in peer-reviewed trials, so treat them as a coaching philosophy.
Use micro-checks throughout the day rather than one long session.

lessons.title: Pogo Hops & Elastic Wall Bounces: Find Your Spring
lessons.summary: Kangaroos hop further than their leg muscles alone can explain, because their tendons and fascia work like springs. Small, quiet, bouncy movements train that same spring in you.
lessons.body_markdown:
## The catapult inside you

Kangaroos hop further and faster than the force of their leg muscles alone can explain. Researchers found a **catapult mechanism**: the tendons and fascia of the legs are tensioned like elastic bands, and releasing that stored energy powers the hop. Gazelles use the same trick, leaping spectacularly without especially powerful muscles. Müller and Schleip describe how high-resolution ultrasound has revealed the same kind of springiness in humans, in hopping, running and even walking.

During bouncy movements, the muscle fibres stay almost the same length while the fascial and tendon elements lengthen and shorten **"like an elastic yoyo spring."** That's why bouncing trains something different from slow lifting.

This is the heart of Chong Xie's message too: **fascia-driven** movement versus muscle-driven movement. Watch his *Hyperarch Hop* and *Wall Bounce* videos for his versions.

## How to do it

### Level 1: Elastic wall bounce (Müller & Schleip)

1. Stand about an arm's length or a bit more from a wall, feet hip-width.
2. Lean forward with a long, tall body and catch yourself on the wall with your hands.
3. Bounce softly off the wall back to standing, then let yourself fall forward again.
4. Keep the whole body pre-tensioned, like a plank. Don't collapse into a "banana" posture.
5. **Make as little sound as possible.** No abrupt movements.

### Level 2: Pogo hops (two feet)

1. Stand tall, feet hip-width, weight toward the balls of the feet.
2. Make small, quick hops of a few centimetres. Mostly ankles, knees only slightly soft.
3. Think "springy and stiff," not "squat and jump." Bounce off the ground like it's hot.
4. Land quietly. Stay tall. Arms relaxed.

### Optional: Rebounding

If you own a mini-trampoline (rebounder), gentle bouncing on it is a lower-impact way to start exploring rhythm and springiness before moving to the floor.

## Sets & timing

- **Wall bounces:** 2–3 sets of 10–15 bounces.
- **Pogo hops:** start with 2–3 sets of 10–20 hops, resting 30–60 seconds between sets.
- **Frequency:** 2 times per week at first. Müller and Schleip suggest fascial training stimulus only once or twice a week, because in tendons collagen breakdown outweighs synthesis for the first 1–2 days after exercise, and synthesis wins afterwards.
- **Stop the set as soon as you lose the spring.** When it gets loud or heavy, you're done.

## Progressions

1. Wall bounce → bounce off a table or windowsill (a lower surface means more load). Only progress once the movement is silent and smooth.
2. Two-foot pogo in place → pogo forward and back → side to side.
3. Two feet → **single-leg pogo** (only once two-foot is easy and quiet).
4. Skipping, then light springy running.

## Why it works

- **Fascial Fitness principles:** elastic recoil and the **ninja principle**, moving as smoothly and quietly as possible, with gradual deceleration before a change of direction and gradual acceleration after it, and no jerky movements.
- **Tendons adapt to bouncing.** In a 14-week study, plyometric (jump) training reduced the energy lost in the Achilles tendon (its *dissipation coefficient* dropped about 35%). The authors conclude that this enhances the transmission of muscular force (Fouré et al., 2010).
- **Different from isometric strength work.** Kubo et al. (2017) compared 12 weeks of plyometric and isometric calf training. Plyometrics increased active muscle stiffness and tendon extensibility during ballistic contractions, changes the authors link to better stretch-shortening performance.
- **It's in the foot too.** Toe and foot strength (Lesson 1) relate to rebound jump performance. Your foundation feeds your spring.

## Common mistakes

- **Loud, heavy landings.** Noise means collapse and wasted energy.
- **Heels slamming down** on every hop.
- **Turning it into a squat jump.** Keep the knees only slightly bent.
- **Too much, too soon.** Tendons adapt more slowly than muscles. Soreness in the Achilles or arch the next day means you overdid it.
- **Banana back** on the wall bounce. Keep the body long and connected.

## Safety note

If you have current Achilles, calf, shin, knee or plantar heel pain, recent ankle sprains, or osteoporosis, get clinical guidance before hopping. Start on a forgiving surface (wood floor, grass, mat), not concrete. Pelvic floor issues can also be aggravated by bouncing, so seek advice if that applies to you.
key_takeaways: Bouncy movements train the body's elastic 'catapult': muscles stay near-isometric while tendons and fascia stretch and recoil.
Quiet, smooth and springy is the cue (the 'ninja principle').
Plyometric training changes Achilles tendon behaviour (Fouré 2010; Kubo 2017).
Start with wall bounces and small two-foot pogos, twice a week, and stop each set when the spring fades.

lessons.title: The Flying Sword: Load the Back Line Like a Bow
lessons.summary: A Fascial Fitness classic. A small counter-movement pre-tensions the long back line, then the body swings forward and back like a catapult. It teaches timing over brute force.
lessons.body_markdown:
## Pull the bow before you shoot

Think about shooting an arrow. You'd never push the arrow with your hand. You pull the bow back, store tension, and release. Müller and Schleip use exactly this image for **preparatory counter-movement**: before the main movement, you pre-tension the fascia in the *opposite* direction so it can recoil.

The **Flying Sword** is their signature exercise for this. It loads the long chain down the back of the body (Myers' **Superficial Back Line**), which a dissection-based review found strong evidence for as a continuous anatomical line.

## How to do it

1. **Set up.** Stand with feet about hip-width (or one foot slightly forward), knees soft. Clasp your hands together as if holding a sword handle, arms extended overhead.
2. **Tension the bow.** Lengthen upward through your arms and spine and tilt your whole body axis *slightly backward* for a brief moment. This is the counter-movement.
3. **Swing forward and down.** Let your upper body and arms spring forward and down like a catapult, as if swinging a sword, folding at the hips with a long spine. Knees can bend.
4. **Catapult back up.** At the bottom, give a small, brief dynamic bounce downward, then let the body swing elastically back up to standing. Müller and Schleip describe briefly activating the muscles on the front of the body first, which loads the back fascia so the recoil does the lifting.
5. **Find the rhythm.** Like playing with a yoyo, you're looking for the ideal swing. You'll know you've found it when the action is **fluid and pleasurable**.

Watch Robert Schleip's *Fascial Fitness (English)* video for the general style and feel.

## Sets & timing

- **2–3 sets of 6–10 swings.**
- 2 times per week as part of your fascial session.
- Rest whenever the movement loses its smoothness.

## Progressions

1. **Small range, slow speed** → **bigger range, natural rhythm.**
2. **Add a diagonal:** swing down toward one foot, then the other. This brings in more of the spiral and functional lines.
3. **Light load:** Müller and Schleip note that free weights can also be used. Hold a light dumbbell or kettlebell only once the unloaded version is smooth.
4. Combine with Lesson 3: a few pogo hops, then the Flying Sword, to feel the elastic theme across your whole body.

## Why it works

- **Preparatory counter-movement increases elastic recoil.** It's one of the core principles in Schleip and Müller's 2013 paper on fascia-oriented training.
- **Timing, not muscle.** The goal is for the stored elastic energy in the back fascia to do the work. Muscle-only lifting misses that.
- **Long lines.** The swing loads the tissue from your heels and calves through the hamstrings, back and up to your head as one chain, rather than isolating a muscle.
- **Real-world transfer.** Throwing, striking, swinging and jumping all use a counter-movement before the main action. This drill rehearses that pattern in its simplest form.

## Common mistakes

- **Muscling it.** If you're grinding up with your lower back, slow down and find the swing.
- **Rounding and collapsing the spine** at the bottom. Fold from the hips with a long spine.
- **Jerky bounces.** The bounce at the bottom is small and smooth, not a yank.
- **Holding your breath.** Breathe out on the way down, in on the way up.
- **Going too big too fast.** Range comes with practice.

## Safety note

This is a dynamic forward bend. If you have current low-back pain, a disc problem, uncontrolled high blood pressure, glaucoma, or get dizzy bending forward, skip it or get clinical advice first. Keep the range small and come up slowly if you feel light-headed.
key_takeaways: Preparatory counter-movement is like pulling a bow: pre-tension the tissue in the opposite direction, then let it recoil.
The Flying Sword loads the Superficial Back Line, a myofascial chain with strong anatomical evidence.
Look for a fluid, pleasurable swing. Timing beats muscle.
2–3 sets of 6–10 swings, twice a week; add diagonals and light weight later.

lessons.title: The Big Cat Stretch & Octopus Leg: Slow Stretches Through Long Lines
lessons.summary: Instead of stretching one muscle at a time, stretch like a cat: long, slow, multi-directional movements that pull through entire fascial chains, plus a slow-motion leg exploration to wake up your body-sense.
lessons.body_markdown:
## Stretch the chain, not the muscle

Watch a cat wake up. It doesn't do a hamstring stretch. It reaches its front paws forward and its hips back at the same time, lengthening its whole body in opposite directions. That's the model for **slow dynamic stretching** in Fascial Fitness.

Müller and Schleip recommend focusing slow dynamic stretches on the **long myofascial chains**. Instead of waiting passively in one position, you explore with slight changes in angle: sideways, diagonals and spiralling rotations. That way large areas of the fascial network are worked at once.

## How to do it

### Part A: The Big Cat Stretch

1. **Start on hands and knees,** or standing with hands on a wall or table at hip height.
2. **Reach in two directions.** Send your fingertips forward and your sit bones back, lengthening from fingertips to sit bones and from tailbone to the crown of your head. If you're standing, reach your heels into the floor too.
3. **Move slowly and steadily.** Change the angle slightly: reach a little more to the left, then to the right, then diagonally. Each change finds a new part of the web.
4. **Add rotation.** Rotate your pelvis or chest toward one side. Feel the stretch spread along that whole side of the body, then gently reverse.
5. **Notice the after-feeling.** Müller and Schleip point to a feeling of increased length afterwards.

### Part B: The Octopus Leg

1. Lie on your back or stand holding a wall for balance.
2. Imagine your leg is an octopus tentacle.
3. In **slow motion**, explore lots of different lengthening movements through the whole leg: turning the foot in and out, reaching through the heel, then the toes, small circles, tiny shifts at the hip.
4. Vary what you activate. The point is novelty and sensation, not range.
5. Switch legs.

## Sets & timing

- **Big Cat Stretch:** 3–5 slow "explorations" of 30–60 seconds each, covering different angles and both sides.
- **Octopus Leg:** 1–2 minutes per leg.
- **Total:** about 5–8 minutes, 2 times per week, or as a daily wind-down.

## Progressions

1. Hands on a table → hands on the floor (more range).
2. Add **fast dynamic stretching** once you're warm: gentle, rhythmic mini-bounces at the end of the range. Müller and Schleip note that this "bouncing stretch" was long considered harmful, but its merits have been confirmed in contemporary research when done warm and without jerking.
3. Add a **preparatory counter-movement:** for example, before lengthening the hip flexors forward, make a brief movement backward first.
4. Try the Octopus with eyes closed to heighten your body-sense.

## Why it works

- **Chains are real.** A systematic review of 62 dissection studies (Wilke et al., 2016) found strong evidence for three myofascial meridians (the Superficial Back Line and the Back and Front Functional Lines) and moderate-to-strong evidence for parts of the Spiral and Lateral Lines. The authors concluded that most skeletal muscles are directly linked by connective tissue.
- **Stretching one area may affect another.** In a small pilot study of 26 people, static stretching of the calves and hamstrings increased neck range of motion. The authors read this as preliminary evidence for strain transfer along myofascial chains (Wilke et al., 2016). It's early research, but it's intriguing.
- **Different tissues need different loading.** Müller and Schleip explain that classic passive stretches mainly load the fascial tissue running parallel to the muscle fibres. Actively loaded stretches at long ranges reach most of the fascial components.
- **Proprioception.** The superficial fascial layers are more densely populated with sensory nerve endings than deeper tissue. The Octopus Leg's slow, varied micro-movements are designed to refine that sense, what Schleip and Müller call **proprioceptive refinement**.

## Common mistakes

- **Static waiting.** Keep moving slowly and keep changing angles.
- **Chasing pain.** You want a strong, pleasant stretch sensation, never sharp pain.
- **Bouncing cold.** Fast dynamic stretches only after warming up, and never jerky.
- **Rushing the Octopus.** Slower is better.

## Safety note

If you're hypermobile, aim for control and sensation, not more range. People who are pregnant, recovering from surgery, or have joint instability should get clinical advice before end-range stretching.
key_takeaways: Stretch whole chains with slow, multi-directional, cat-like reaching rather than isolated static holds.
Dissection research supports several myofascial lines (Wilke et al., 2016).
Pilot data suggest stretching the legs can change neck range of motion, early evidence for strain transfer.
Use slow-motion leg exploration (Octopus) to refine proprioception.

lessons.title: Spiral Reach & Rotation: Wake Up the Spiral Line
lessons.summary: Athletes throw, swing, punch and cut by rotating. A simple standing spiral-reach routine trains the diagonal and spiral connections that link your foot to your opposite shoulder.
lessons.body_markdown:
## Athletes move in spirals

A tennis serve. A punch. A golf swing. A sprinter's arms swinging against their legs. Almost every powerful athletic movement involves rotation, with force travelling diagonally across the body.

In Thomas Myers' Anatomy Trains map, the **Spiral Line** wraps around the body in a double helix, linking the skull and neck across the upper back to the opposite shoulder and ribs, across the belly to the hip, and down the leg to the arch of the foot. The **Functional Lines** cross the front and back of the torso, connecting each shoulder to the opposite hip. A dissection-based review found strong evidence for the front and back functional lines and moderate-to-strong evidence for parts of the spiral line.

Gym machines mostly work in straight lines. This lesson adds the missing dimension.

## How to do it

### 1. Standing spiral reach

1. Stand in your **Feet Straight** stance from Lesson 2, feet hip-width, inside ankles high.
2. Reach your **right arm** up and across your body toward the upper left, as if reaching for a high shelf on your left.
3. Let the movement spiral down through your body: ribs turn, pelvis follows slightly, and you feel the stretch run from your right hand, across your back and side, toward your left hip and leg.
4. Keep both feet rooted, and feel the arches hold.
5. Return slowly and repeat to the other side.

### 2. Counter-movement rotations

1. Arms relaxed, soft knees.
2. Turn slightly to the **left** first (the counter-movement), then let your body swing to the **right** like a door on a spring. Arms wrap loosely around you.
3. Swing back the other way. Build a smooth, rhythmic, effortless swing.
4. Let the movement start from the ground. Feet stay connected, and the heel of the back foot may lift slightly as the hips turn.

### 3. Diagonal Flying Sword (optional)

Use the Flying Sword from Lesson 4, but swing down toward one foot, then the other.

## Sets & timing

- **Spiral reach:** 5–8 slow reps per side, pausing 2–3 seconds at the end of the reach.
- **Counter-movement rotations:** 2 sets of 20–30 easy swings.
- 2 times per week, or as a warm-up before sport.

## Progressions

1. Small range → full range.
2. Slow → rhythmic and springy (swings).
3. **Step-through spiral:** step forward with the left foot while reaching the right arm across. Walking is a rotation pattern too.
4. **Lunge with rotation:** in a split stance, rotate the torso over the front leg slowly. Keep the front foot straight and arch lifted.
5. Explore Chong Xie's *Push Hands* video for a martial-arts take on whole-body connected force.

## Why it works

- **The diagonal connections exist.** Wilke et al. (2016) reviewed 62 dissection studies and verified continuity for the Back and Front Functional Lines and parts of the Spiral Line.
- **Counter-movement + rotation = elastic recoil.** The same catapult principle from Lessons 3 and 4, applied rotationally. Müller and Schleip specifically recommend sideways, diagonal and spiralling variations to involve large areas of the fascial network.
- **Connecting top and bottom.** Running the spiral from hand to opposite foot trains the idea at the centre of this course: the body works as one connected unit, not a stack of separate parts.

An honest note: the *anatomy* of these lines is well documented. How much training them as lines improves sport performance is still being researched. That's why Josh frames it as his lived experience: training through the lines changed how his body moves.

## Common mistakes

- **Twisting only from the lower back.** Let the rotation spread through ribs, hips and feet.
- **Feet spinning out or arches collapsing.** Stay rooted.
- **Forcing range.** Rotation should feel easy and springy.
- **Holding your breath.** Breathe out as you reach.

## Safety note

If you have current back pain, a disc problem, or recent rib or abdominal surgery, keep the range small and pain-free, or get clinical advice first. Rotation under load (weights) should come only after the bodyweight version is smooth.
key_takeaways: Athletic power is often rotational; the spiral and functional lines connect each shoulder to the opposite hip and leg.
Dissection evidence supports the front and back functional lines strongly and parts of the spiral line moderately.
Use counter-movement swings for elastic, effortless rotation.
Keep feet rooted and let rotation spread through the whole body, not just the lower back.

lessons.title: Crawl & Hang: Ground and Overhead
lessons.summary: Crawling connects hands, feet and core into one diagonal pattern; hanging loads the hands, shoulders and trunk overhead. Two primal positions most adults have abandoned.
lessons.body_markdown:
## Positions you've forgotten

As kids, we all crawled, climbed and hung from things. Most adults now spend their day sitting, then train in a few fixed gym positions. The tissue adapts to that narrow menu.

Müller and Schleip's **proprioceptive refinement** principle encourages placing the body in **unfamiliar positions** and varying movement qualities, because the nervous system filters out repetitive, predictable input. Crawling and hanging are two of the simplest ways to give your body new information.

## Part A: The crawl

### How to do it

1. **Start on hands and knees.** Hands under shoulders, knees under hips, fingers spread.
2. **Lift your knees 2–5 cm off the floor.** Your back stays flat, like a table.
3. **Move opposite hand and foot together:** right hand + left foot, then left hand + right foot.
4. **Small steps, slow and quiet.** Keep the hips level. Don't let them sway.
5. **Breathe normally.**

This contralateral (opposite arm/leg) pattern is the same cross-body coordination you use when you walk and run, which is why it pairs with the functional lines from Lesson 6.

Watch the GOATA *Cat Crawl* to see one system's version.

### Sets & timing
- 3–4 rounds of 20–30 seconds (or 5–10 steps forward and back), resting as needed.

### Progressions
1. Hold the hover position only (no moving) → crawl forward → backward → sideways.
2. Slower is harder: try 3 seconds per step.
3. Longer distances once you can keep the back flat and hips quiet.

## Part B: The hang

### How to do it

1. Use a sturdy pull-up bar, monkey bars or a secure doorframe bar.
2. **Start with feet on the floor or a box** so you're only partly hanging. This is the beginner version.
3. Grip the bar with hands about shoulder-width.
4. **Passive hang:** let the shoulders rise toward the ears and breathe, feeling the stretch through hands, arms, armpits, sides and back.
5. **Active hang:** gently pull the shoulders down away from the ears without bending the elbows.
6. Step down with control.

### Sets & timing
- 3–5 hangs of 10–30 seconds, building up gradually over weeks.

### Progressions
1. Feet-supported hang → full bodyweight hang.
2. Passive → active → alternating between them.
3. Gentle side-to-side sway, letting the stretch travel down one side of the body.

## Why it works

- **Hands are a foot, upstairs.** Chong Xie has a video dedicated to training the fascia of the hands: *How To Start Training My Hand Fascia*. Crawling and hanging both load the hands and fingers.
- **Novel positions refine your body-sense.** Müller and Schleip argue for varied and creative movement to prevent the sensory dampening that comes from repetitive patterns.
- **Cross-body coordination.** The crawl rehearses opposite-limb coordination through the trunk, which matches the diagonal connections described in the functional lines.

**Honest note on evidence:** We couldn't find high-quality trials on crawling or hanging as fascia training. Squat University's video below takes a physical therapist's look at what dead hangs do for the shoulders. Treat these as simple, low-risk practices grounded in coaching experience and Josh's philosophy, not as proven treatments.

## Common mistakes

- **Crawl:** hips high in the air, back sagging, or rushing. Keep it low, flat and slow.
- **Crawl:** wrists collapsing. Spread the fingers and press through the whole hand.
- **Hang:** jumping straight into long, full-bodyweight hangs. Build up.
- **Hang:** dropping off the bar. Always step down.

## Safety note

If you have current wrist, elbow or shoulder pain, a history of shoulder dislocation or instability, or recent upper-body surgery, check with a clinician before hanging, and keep the feet supported. Make sure any bar is rated for your weight and securely installed. Crawling on a hard floor can bother sensitive wrists. Start on a mat or grass.
key_takeaways: Crawling trains opposite hand–foot coordination through the trunk, the same cross-body pattern used in walking and running.
Hanging loads the hands, shoulders and sides of the body overhead; start with feet supported.
Unfamiliar positions refine proprioception (a Fascial Fitness principle).
Research on crawling and hanging as fascia training is thin; treat them as simple, low-risk practices.

lessons.title: Slow Rolling: Self-Myofascial Release, the Fascia Way
lessons.summary: Foam rolling is everywhere, and mostly done too fast and too hard. Learn the slow, sponge-like way to roll, what the research really shows, and when not to do it.
lessons.body_markdown:
## Squeeze the sponge

Fascia is largely water. Müller and Schleip describe it as **sponge-like**: when you load or stretch it, fluid is pressed out of the stressed areas. When you release, fresh fluid flows back in from surrounding tissue and the lymphatic and vascular networks.

That's the idea behind fascia-style rolling. You're not "flattening" anything or "breaking up" tissue. You're applying **slow, subtle pressure and release** to encourage that squeeze-and-refill effect, and waking up the sensory nerves in the tissue.

Chong Xie tackles a big question in his video *Fascia Release Or Fascia Strengthening?* Watch it for his answer. In this module, the position is clear: rolling is a tool that supports your training, not the training itself.

## How to do it

**Tools:** a foam roller (soft or medium to start), or a tennis/lacrosse ball for the feet.

### 1. Foot roll (1–2 minutes per foot)
Standing or seated, place a ball under your foot. Slowly roll from heel to toes and side to side with gentle pressure. Pause on tender spots and breathe.

### 2. Calf roll (1–2 minutes per leg)
Sit with the roller under your calf. Use your hands to control how much weight goes on. Move **very slowly**, a centimetre at a time. Turn the leg slightly in and out to change the angle.

### 3. Outer and back of thigh (1–2 minutes per leg)
Lie on your side or sit on the roller. Same rule: slow, small changes in direction and pressure.

### 4. Upper back (1–2 minutes)
Lie with the roller across your upper back, hands supporting your head. Slowly roll a few centimetres, and gently arch over the roller.

### The fascia-style cues

- **Slow motion.** Müller and Schleip recommend only slow-motion, subtle changes in the forces and directions applied.
- **Adjust firmness and body weight** for you. Harder isn't better.
- **Breathe and stay relaxed.** If you're tensing up, it's too much.

## Sets & timing

- **5–10 minutes total**, focusing on 2–4 areas.
- **1–2 minutes per area.**
- Use it before training to feel looser, after training or on rest days to recover, or whenever an area feels stiff.

## Progressions

1. Soft roller → firmer roller.
2. Hands taking weight → more body weight.
3. Rolling → rolling plus slow active movement (for example, slowly bending and straightening the knee while on the roller).

## Why it works, and what it doesn't do

The research is reasonably good here:

- **Short-term flexibility.** A meta-analysis of 26 high-quality trials (Wilke et al., 2020) found foam rolling had a large positive effect on range of motion compared with doing nothing, but it was **not better than stretching**.
- **Soreness and recovery.** A systematic review (Beardsley & Škarabot, 2015) found self-myofascial release seems to increase flexibility and reduce muscle soreness acutely without impeding athletic performance. Evidence for long-term flexibility gains was conflicting.
- **What it isn't.** Rolling is a short-term feel-good and mobility tool. It's not a replacement for the elastic, strength and alignment work in Lessons 1–7.

## Common mistakes

- **Rolling fast, back and forth.** Slow down. Fast rolling misses the point.
- **Grinding on painful spots** until you wince. Gentle pressure, steady breathing.
- **Rolling directly on bones, joints or the lower spine.**
- **Thinking more is better.** A few focused minutes is plenty.

## Safety note

An international expert Delphi study (Bartsch et al., 2021) reached consensus that **open wounds and bone fractures are contraindications** for foam rolling. It also flagged **local tissue inflammation, deep vein thrombosis, osteomyelitis and myositis ossificans** as cautions. Don't roll over swollen, hot, bruised or recently injured areas. If you have a blood-clotting disorder, take blood thinners, have osteoporosis, varicose veins, or a history of DVT, talk to a clinician first. If calf pain comes with swelling, warmth or redness, don't roll it. Get it checked.
key_takeaways: Roll slowly with subtle pressure changes; think 'squeeze and refill a sponge', not 'break up tissue'.
Foam rolling improves short-term range of motion about as well as stretching (Wilke et al., 2020).
It can reduce soreness without hurting performance (Beardsley & Škarabot, 2015), but it supports training rather than replacing it.
Never roll over open wounds or fractures; be cautious with inflammation and any suspected DVT.
